# Reference metadata and claim-support audit

Audit date: 28 September 2026. All thirteen manuscript references were queried directly through the Crossref works API. Eleven resolved. The two arXiv DOIs returned HTTP 404 because they are registered with DataCite; their titles, authors, dates, and primary URLs were verified against DataCite and the arXiv version-one primary pages. This is an explicit registry exception, not a claim that those references were verified by Crossref. Both must be identified as preprints wherever their status matters.

Raw responses and the two Crossref failure-status records are in `scoping/reference_metadata/`. `manuscript/references.json` is CSL JSON rebuilt from those records with `python scoping/reference_metadata/build_csl.py`. These files concern references and published findings, not the study's analysis outcomes. The audit distinguishes verified source claims from the proposed study's interpretations. Any additional manuscript claims need an additional audit entry.

## Metadata verification

| CSL key | Authors and year | Exact title | DOI and registry result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pescetelli2021` | Niccolò Pescetelli; Nicholas Yeung (2021) | The role of decision confidence in advice-taking and trust formation | [10.1037/xge0000960](https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000960), Crossref 200 |
| `jaquiery2024` | Matt Jaquiery; Nick Yeung (2024) | Preferences for advisor agreement and accuracy | [10.1371/journal.pone.0311211](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0311211), Crossref 200 |
| `fetchenhauer2010` | Detlef Fetchenhauer; David Dunning (2010) | Why So Cynical? Asymmetric Feedback Underlies Misguided Skepticism Regarding the Trustworthiness of Others | [10.1177/0956797609358586](https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797609358586), Crossref 200 |
| `denrell2005` | Jerker Denrell (2005) | Why Most People Disapprove of Me: Experience Sampling in Impression Formation | [10.1037/0033-295X.112.4.951](https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.112.4.951), Crossref 200 |
| `honeycutt2020` | Donald R. Honeycutt; Mahsan Nourani; Eric D. Ragan (2020) | Soliciting Human-in-the-Loop User Feedback for Interactive Machine Learning Reduces User Trust and Impressions of Model Accuracy | [10.1609/hcomp.v8i1.7464](https://doi.org/10.1609/hcomp.v8i1.7464), Crossref 200 |
| `denrell2001` | Jerker Denrell; James G. March (2001) | Adaptation as Information Restriction: The Hot Stove Effect | [10.1287/orsc.12.5.523.10092](https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.12.5.523.10092), Crossref 200 |
| `fok2024` | Raymond Fok; Daniel S. Weld (2024) | In search of verifiability: Explanations rarely enable complementary performance in AI-advised decision making | [10.1002/aaai.12182](https://doi.org/10.1002/aaai.12182), Crossref 200 |
| `gao2021` | Ruijiang Gao; Maytal Saar-Tsechansky; Maria De-Arteaga; Ligong Han; Min Kyung Lee; Matthew Lease (2021) | Human-AI Collaboration with Bandit Feedback | [10.24963/ijcai.2021/237](https://doi.org/10.24963/ijcai.2021/237), Crossref 200 |
| `zavattari2026` | Cesare Zavattari; Alessandro Tommasi; Giuseppe Prencipe (2026) | One Human, N Agents: Audit-Budget Allocation for LLM Agent Fleets under Miscalibrated, Correlated Confidence | [10.48550/arXiv.2607.28317](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2607.28317), Crossref 404; DataCite 200; arXiv v1 dated 30 July 2026 |
| `li2026` | ZhaoBin Li; Mark Steyvers (2026) | Learning to Trust: How Humans Mentally Recalibrate AI Confidence Signals | [10.48550/arXiv.2603.22634](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2603.22634), Crossref 404; DataCite 200; arXiv v1 dated 23 March 2026 |

Metadata conventions: Pescetelli and Yeung appeared online in 2020, but Crossref identifies the journal issue as March 2021, volume 150(3), 507–526; the bibliography uses 2021. Crossref supplies “Nicholas” for this paper and “Nick” for Jaquiery and Yeung. Fetchenhauer and Dunning's subtitle is a separate Crossref field and has been included. Honeycutt and Ragan's middle initials and issue 1 are supplied by the primary publisher page because Crossref omits them. Fok and Weld's correct pagination is 317–332 in volume 45(3). Gao et al. appear on pages 1722–1728 of the Thirtieth IJCAI proceedings. Dollar signs around N in arXiv's title are TeX formatting and are removed from CSL display text. Minor case and hyphen typography differences do not change titles.

## Claim-to-source audit

### Pescetelli and Yeung (2021)

**Claim supported:** Confidence-weighted agreement can inform advisor evaluations without feedback, but correlated judgments undermine its validity.

**Source and location:** [Oxford primary accepted manuscript and bibliographic record](https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid%3A5b00b576-d379-437d-bd71-91eeedd89f17), abstract and Experiment 2. The record explicitly describes feedback versus feedback-free comparisons and agent-based simulations.

**Boundary:** This already models confidence, dependence, and trust. It does not establish the consequences of revealing ground truth selectively on disagreements, or the proposed absolute-versus-paired display intervention. No source-based numerical estimate is carried into the manuscript from this audit.

### Jaquiery and Yeung (2024)

**Claim supported:** Advisor choice reflects both accuracy and agreement; objective feedback strengthens preference for accuracy in their experimental contrasts.

**Source and location:** [PLOS primary full text](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0311211), Abstract; Materials and methods, Task overview and Dates Task; Discussion. Methods describe feedback at the end of trials in the relevant conditions, rather than a manipulation selecting feedback by disagreement.

**Boundary:** Do not assert that accuracy lost to agreement on average in their no-feedback direct comparison. The paper instead reports wide individual differences. Our distinction concerns which completed cases generate labelled feedback.

### Fetchenhauer and Dunning (2010)

**Claim supported:** Giving feedback regardless of participants' trust decisions reduced their underestimation of others' trustworthiness relative to asymmetric or absent feedback.

**Source and location:** [Author-hosted primary article](https://sites.lsa.umich.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/275/2015/11/fetchdunnps10.pdf), abstract and experiment; Crossref abstract independently confirms the comparison.

**Boundary:** The outcome is interpersonal reciprocity. This supports the broader relevance of selected experience, not the claim that the present classification model empirically explains their participants.

### Gao et al. (2021)

**Claim supported:** Human–AI policy learning under bandit feedback uses inverse-propensity weighting to address action selection in logged outcomes and to optimise routing between humans and an algorithm.

**Source and location:** [Primary proceedings PDF](https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2021/0237.pdf), §2 Counterfactual Policy Optimization (p. 1723); §3 Counterfactual Risk Minimization, equations 2–3, and Collaboration Objective, equation 4 (p. 1724). §1 explains that rewards are observed only for actions actually taken. §2 explicitly distinguishes the system from human–machine interaction.

**Boundary:** IPW and the general selective-outcome problem are established methods, not contributions of this study. Gao et al. learn policies from action-dependent rewards. The present model compares representations of selectively labelled classification cases, where one revealed ground-truth label evaluates both already-made predictions. It neither solves their general bandit problem nor estimates missing causal rewards.

### Zavattari et al. (2026), preprint

**Claim supported:** The preprint studies how to allocate a limited audit budget across an agent fleet with miscalibrated confidence and correlated errors, comparing audit policies by residual undetected errors.

**Source and location:** [Primary arXiv full text, v1](https://arxiv.org/html/…211 tokens truncated…Primary publisher page](https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/10.1287/orsc.12.5.523.10092), abstract; also saved Crossref abstract.

**Boundary:** Cite for the established mechanism of restricted experience. Do not present adaptive sampling bias as a new general mechanism established here.

### Denrell (2005)

**Claim supported:** Impression-dependent interaction can make early negative impressions more persistent by reducing further interaction.

**Source and location:** [Primary article DOI](https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.112.4.951), abstract and model overview; author-uploaded article text was inspected in the scoping pass. Bibliographic identity was independently verified through Crossref.

**Boundary:** This is a foundation for the role of experience sampling, not direct evidence about AI verification displays.

### Honeycutt et al. (2020)

**Claim supported:** Providing feedback in a simulated object-detection interaction lowered reported trust and perceived accuracy, whether or not system accuracy improved.

**Source and location:** [Primary AAAI publisher page](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/HCOMP/article/view/7464), Abstract; saved Crossref abstract.

**Boundary:** This audit verified the published abstract, not every experimental design detail. Do not identify disagreement-selected feedback as the demonstrated cause of the effect.

### Fok and Weld (2024)

**Claim supported:** The authors argue that explanations support complementary decision performance insofar as they permit verification of predictions.

**Source and location:** [Primary publisher full text](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/aaai.12182), Abstract and Introduction; [author preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.07722).

**Boundary:** This is a theoretical argument, not a universal empirical demonstration that every useful explanation works only through verification. The proposed study assumes a successful verification channel and examines what its selected history permits a learner to infer.

### Li and Steyvers (2026), preprint

**Claim supported:** Participants can learn mappings between AI confidence and correctness across repeated labelled feedback, and the authors model adjustment of baseline trust and confidence sensitivity.

**Source and location:** [Primary arXiv full text, v1](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.22634v1), Experiment, Materials and Procedure; Cognitive Modeling, Linear-in-Log-Odds Calibration and Rescorla–Wagner Learning Rule. The latter explicitly states that correctness feedback follows every trial.

**Boundary:** Their learning model concerns calibration with trialwise feedback. The present selective-feedback model does not show that their estimated parameters generalise to missing labels, nor establish the proposed paired tracker as a human cognitive mechanism.

## Citation-use checks required at manuscript completion

- Cite empirical sources for the limited finding audited here, and distinguish the study's formal derivations and predictions from those sources' findings.
- Do not use registry resolution as evidence that a substantive claim is supported: metadata identity and claim support are separate checks.
- Keep both 2026 works labelled as preprints; record Crossref's 404 results without suppressing relevant competing work.
- Treat the paired-disagreement sign identity as an elementary analytic property, not a priority claim.
- Published-source numeric results were read during literature review, but no participant-level outcome file was downloaded or analysed for this audit.

## Foundational additions from manuscript review

The bibliography now contains twelve entries: ten Crossref-resolved references and two DataCite-registered arXiv preprints. The original raw metadata are retained. APA display titles use sentence case through an explicit mapping in the bibliography builder, preserving AI, LLM, and the mathematical N.

### Einhorn and Hogarth (1978), `einhorn1978`

**Verified metadata:** Hillel J. Einhorn and Robin M. Hogarth. *Confidence in judgment: Persistence of the illusion of validity.* *Psychological Review, 85*(5), 395–416. DOI [10.1037/0033-295X.85.5.395](https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.85.5.395). Crossref HTTP 200; raw response saved.

**Narrow supported claim:** Learning about one's judgement depends on task structure, which action outcomes can be observed, and how feedback is coded and interpreted. The authors explain how action-contingent observation can obstruct disconfirmation and maintain confidence.

**Primary evidence:** [Published article PDF hosted by an academic lab](https://worthylab.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/einhorn_hogarth_1978.pdf), pp. 396–398, “Task Structure and Psychological Process”, including the hiring example where rejected candidates' outcomes are unavailable. This supports the foundational distinction between experience and useful evidence, not a claim that the present feedback-display intervention was tested in 1978.

### McNemar (1947), `mcnemar1947`

**Verified metadata:** Quinn McNemar. *Note on the sampling error of the difference between correlated proportions or percentages.* *Psychometrika, 12*(2), 153–157. DOI [10.1007/BF02295996](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02295996). Crossref HTTP 200; raw response saved.

**Narrow supported claim:** Comparison of correlated proportions has a classical statistical foundation in McNemar's paper. The primary publisher abstract describes significance formulas and their chi-square connection.

**Primary evidence and access limit:** [Springer primary record](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02295996), Abstract. The original full text was subscription restricted; this audit does not claim direct inspection of its discordant-cell formula. In the manuscript, cite as historical grounding for correlated-proportion comparisons, while deriving the agreement-zero identity directly. Do not say McNemar studied selective verification or advisor learning.

"""Reviewer verification: exact focal risks without importing production code.

Builds joint tables using rational arithmetic and convolves integer score
increments. The only floating error in the benchmark is probability arithmetic;
there is no Monte Carlo approximation. All focal rows, including random audits,
are checked against this benchmark and independently scored saved histories.
"""
import hashlib
import json
from fractions import Fraction as F
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]


def rational_probabilities(env, schedule, config):
    p, r = F(str(env['p'])), F(str(env['r']))
    masses = []
    for share, h, a in [(p, config['h_low'], env['a_low']),
                         (1-p, config['h_high'], env['a_high'])]:
        h, a = F(str(h)), F(str(a))
        joint = max(F(0), h+a-1) * (1-r) + min(h, a) * r
        masses.extend(share*x for x in [joint, h-joint, a-joint, 1-h-a+joint])
    h = p*F(str(config['h_low'])) + (1-p)*F(str(config['h_high']))
    a = p*F(str(env['a_low'])) + (1-p)*F(str(env['a_high']))
    k = 1 if schedule == 'random' else int(schedule[1:])
    selected = masses if schedule == 'random' else [
        x*(F(1,k) if j < 4 else 1) if j % 4 in (1, 2) else F(0)
        for j, x in enumerate(masses)]
    audit_yield = sum(selected)
    assert all(x >= 0 for x in masses) and sum(masses) == 1
    return np.array([float(x/audit_yield) for x in selected]), h, a-h, float(audit_yield)


def increments(learner, schedule, human):
    k = 1 if schedule == 'random' else int(schedule[1:])
    # Signs of rational scores can be evaluated exactly as integer sums.
    if learner == 'absolute':
        return np.array([human.denominator*x-human.numerator
                         for x in (1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0)], dtype=int)
    low_weight = k if learner == 'ipw' else min(k, 2) if learner == 'capped' else 1
    return np.array([0, -low_weight, low_weight, 0, 0, -1, 1, 0])


def exact_risk(prob, steps, n, delta):
    lower, upper = int(steps.min()), int(steps.max())
    kernel = np.zeros(upper-lower+1)
    np.add.at(kernel, steps-lower, prob)
    distribution = np.array([1.0])
    for _ in range(n):
        distribution = np.convolve(distribution, kernel)
    scores = np.arange(len(distribution)) + n*lower
    adoption = (scores > 0).astype(float) + .5*(scores == 0)
    loss = abs(float(delta)) * (1-adoption if delta > 0 else adoption)
    assert abs(distribution.sum()-1) < 1e-11
    return float(distribution @ loss), float(distribution @ adoption)


def main():
    config = json.loads((ROOT/'config.json').read_text())
    cells = json.loads((ROOT/'output/cells.json').read_text())
    summary = pd.read_csv(ROOT/'output/summary.csv')
    contrasts = json.loads((ROOT/'output/contrasts.json').read_text())
    checks, exact = [], {}
    raw_contrasts = {}
    with np.load(ROOT/'output/raw_counts.npz', allow_pickle=False) as raw:
        for cell in cells:
            if not cell['environment']['focal']:
                continue
            env, schedule, n = cell['environment'], cell['schedule'], cell['n']
            prob, human, delta, audit_yield = rational_probabilities(env, schedule, config)
            assert np.allclose(prob, cell['audit_probability'], atol=1e-14, rtol=0)
            assert abs(audit_yield-cell['audit_yield']) < 1e-14
            counts = raw[cell['key']].astype(np.int64)
            risks = {}
            for learner in ('absolute', 'paired', 'ipw', 'capped'):
                steps = increments(learner, schedule, human)
                risk, adoption = exact_risk(prob, steps, n, delta)
                key = (env['env_id'], schedule, n, learner)
                exact[key] = risk
                numerators = counts @ steps
                adopted = (numerators > 0).astype(float) + .5*(numerators == 0)
                losses = abs(float(delta)) * (1-adopted if delta > 0 else adopted)
                risks[learner] = losses
                row = summary[(summary.env_id == env['env_id']) &
                              (summary.schedule == schedule) & (summary.n == n) &
                              (summary.learner == learner)].iloc[0]
                raw_mcse = float(losses.std(ddof=1)/np.sqrt(len(losses)))
                assert abs(losses.mean()-row.regret) < 1e-14
                assert abs(adopted.mean()-row.adoption) < 1e-14
                assert abs(raw_mcse-row.regret_mcse) < 1e-14
                tolerance = 5*raw_mcse + 1e-4
                passed = abs(risk-row.regret) <= tolerance
                assert passed, (key, risk, row.regret)
                checks.append(dict(environment=env['env_id'], schedule=schedule,
                    n=n, learner=learner, exact_regret=risk,
                    exact_adoption=adoption, simulated_regret=float(row.regret),
                    mcse=raw_mcse, error=float(row.regret-risk),
                    tolerance=tolerance, passed=bool(passed)))
            raw_diff = risks['ipw']-risks['paired']
            raw_contrasts[(env['env_id'], schedule, n)] = (
                float(raw_diff.mean()), float(raw_diff.std(ddof=1)/np.sqrt(len(raw_diff))))
    primary = []
    for contrast in contrasts:
        key = (contrast['env_id'], contrast['schedule'], contrast['n'])
        exact_diff = exact[(*key, 'ipw')]-exact[(*key, 'paired')]
        raw_mean, raw_se = raw_contrasts[key]
        assert abs(raw_mean-contrast['mean']) < 1e-14
        assert abs(raw_se-contrast['mcse']) < 1e-14
        interval_contains = contrast['ci_low'] <= exact_diff <= contrast['ci_high']
        assert abs(exact_diff-raw_mean) <= 5*raw_se+1e-4
        primary.append(dict(hypothesis=contrast['hypothesis'], exact_contrast=exact_diff,
            simulated_contrast=raw_mean, mcse=raw_se,
            difference_in_mcse=(raw_mean-exact_diff)/raw_se,
            exact_inside_registered_interval=bool(interval_contains)))
    report = dict(passed=True, method='Independent rational joint tables; n-fold discrete convolution of integer score increments; independently scored saved focal histories',
        simulation_imports=False, focal_learner_checks=len(checks), primary=primary,
        checks=checks, source_sha256=hashlib.sha256(Path(__file__).read_bytes()).hexdigest())
    (ROOT/'output/independent_check.json').write_text(json.dumps(report, indent=2)+'\n')
    print(json.dumps({k:v for k,v in report.items() if k != 'checks'}, indent=2))


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
"}

Search completed 28 September 2026; primary sources, queries, metadata, and caveats are preserved in `scoping/literature_agent.md` and `scoping/journal_and_data.md`. This is a scoped search, not proof that no prior paper contains the same result. No hypothesis-bearing simulation or participant-level outcome was examined.

## Study contribution

The paper distinguishes two targets of learning from selectively verified advice: absolute advisor accuracy and the sign of the advisor's accuracy advantage over oneself. It derives the limits of paired comparison and quantifies finite-feedback decision loss when correction for confidence selection trades reduced bias for additional variance. A future randomised feedback-display experiment supplies refutable psychological predictions. The mathematical identity, inverse-probability weighting, and the general fact that selection biases learning are existing ideas, not claimed inventions.

## Five closest papers

1. **Pescetelli & Yeung (2021), The role of decision confidence in advice-taking and trust formation.** DOI: https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000960. Their experiments and models concern confidence-weighted agreement as evidence of advisor reliability, including learning without objective feedback and distortion from dependent judgements. **Addition:** objective truth is available but selectively sampled; compare absolute and paired representations of the same verified cases and state their different estimands. This is not the first computational model of confidence and trust.

2. **Jaquiery & Yeung (2024), Preferences for advisor agreement and accuracy.** DOI: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0311211. Their experiments distinguish agreement and accuracy with and without feedback; feedback supports preference for accuracy. **Addition:** distinguish feedback's presence from its selection mechanism; uniform disagreement feedback can remain adequate for relative ranking even when inappropriate for absolute assessment. No claim that their participants exhibited the proposed selection effect.

3. **Fetchenhauer & Dunning (2010), Why so cynical? Asymmetric feedback underlies misguided skepticism regarding the trustworthiness of others.** DOI: https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797609358586. Their trust experiments show that feedback conditional on trusting can sustain inaccurate negative impressions. **Addition:** advisor verification offers a paired contrast whose unobserved values on agreement are structurally zero, so missing feedback need not undermine the comparative decision. Reciprocity and classification accuracy are distinct tasks; this paper does not reproduce their experiment.

4. **Gao et al. (2021), Human-AI Collaboration with Bandit Feedback.** DOI: https://doi.org/10.24963/ijcai.2021/237. They use counterfactual policy learning to route cases between humans and machines under bandit feedback. **Addition:** a constrained global advisor-adoption decision, with fully verified paired labels on sampled cases, psychologically interpretable absolute/paired summaries, and finite-label cost of selection adjustment. IPW itself and learning from selectively observed outcomes are established; no general policy-learning advance is claimed.

5. **Zavattari, Tommasi, & Prencipe (2026), One Human, N Agents: Audit-Budget Allocation for LLM Agent Fleets under Miscalibrated, Correlated Confidence.** Primary preprint: https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28317. It already models budgeted inspections, confidence selection, correlated errors, and worse-than-random auditing. **Addition:** learning comparative competence from a feedback history rather than allocating inspections to reduce remaining errors across a fleet; paired representation and the zero contribution of agreements are central. This is an unreviewed preprint, and its DOI belongs to DataCite rather than Crossref; registry coverage must not be misrepresented.

## Further overlap and limits

Denrell & March (2001) and Denrell (2005) already explain biased impressions through selective experience. Fok & Weld (2024) discuss verification and complementary performance. Honeycutt et al. (2020) show that interactive feedback can reduce trust and perceived accuracy. Li & Steyvers (2026, preprint) model learning AI confidence calibration. These precedents restrict the contribution to a particular representation-by-selection boundary and its finite-feedback consequences.

A transparent two-stratum scenario is intentionally limited. The paper cannot establish which summaries humans use, how often real verification follows the assumed policies, or that its numerical worlds describe deployed AI. It should be judged as a computational Theory Article with a testable behavioural extension, not as empirical evidence of algorithm aversion.

## Post-preregistration literature addendum: selective-feedback coding

Added during the first manuscript review, after preregistration and confirmatory analysis, on 28 September 2026. This supplements the original five-paper assessment without changing the preregistration or the simulations.

**Elwin, Juslin, Olsson, and Enkvist (2007), Constructivist coding: Learning from selective feedback**, [10.1111/j.1467-9280.2007.01856.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2007.01856.x), is a substantive predecessor. Their investment task contrasted complete with decision-contingent feedback. Performance was not demonstrably impaired by selective feedback, and behaviour was better captured by reconstructing missing outcomes from task knowledge than by merely recording observed outcomes. Their design also approximately matched feedback counts by allowing more training opportunities under selection. Primary full text and Crossref metadata were checked; see `manuscript/reference_audit.md`.

**Implication for contribution:** The general claims that selective experience need not damage decisions, that feedback representation matters, and that label-matched comparisons are useful are already established. This paper's narrower addition concerns absolute advisor accuracy versus the sign of a paired advisor–self accuracy difference, including the zero contribution of agreement cases and the finite-sample consequences of confidence-dependent selection within disagreements. Elwin et al. reconstruct unobserved outcomes for task learning and base-rate inference; the paired source-comparison identity and present estimator comparison are different. Their evidence is also a reason to treat the absolute learner as an experimental benchmark rather than an established default account of human learning.

# Lukas Wallrich -- Academic Writing Style Guide

# PART A: Core Style Rules (always apply)

## Voice and Person
- **Default to "we" or "I"**, never use third person to refer to the researcher(s) or "we" in single-author papers (unless instructed otherwise for peer-review blinding).
- **Active voice** is strongly preferred but passive is acceptable in method sections where the agent is irrelevant.

## Spelling and Conventions
- **British English** by default (behaviour, organisation, standardised, practise, colour, analyse).
- APA formatting conventions followed for empirical papers.
- Oxford comma used consistently.
- Numbers: follows APA convention (words for numbers below 10 at the start of sentences, digits otherwise).

## Hedging and Epistemic Markers
- Claims are carefully **calibrated to match the strength of the evidence**:
  - **Tentative:** "it is possible that", "this suggests that", "might", "may", "appears to"
  - **Moderate:** "this is likely because", "evidently", "it appears clear that"
  - **Confident:** "the evidence clearly favors", "it is clear that"
- Results that disconfirm expectations are reported openly: "Contrary to our expectation..."
- Uses concessive structures naturally: "While X is true, Y is also the case"
- Willing to state when evidence is inconclusive rather than forcing a narrative.
- When editing or rephrasing, the strength of a claim changes only by deliberate decision. Smoothing a sentence can quietly turn "shows" into "suggests" or "may" into "does".

## Vocabulary
- **Academic but accessible**: avoids unnecessarily complex vocabulary while maintaining precision.
- Slightly formal but not stiff; occasional colloquial touches in practitioner-oriented work ("window-dressing", "won't do").
- **Check that a category label covers all its members**: "two selection effects pull in opposite directions" where the second is not a selection effect; "the complementary quantity" followed two sentences later by "the two are not complements"; "bracket the range" for two values that both sit at its top.

### Words and constructions to avoid
- "delve", "crucial", "landscape" (as metaphor), "novel" (for own contribution), "robust" (as generic praise), "pivotal", "tapestry", "interplay", "intricacies"
- "align with" (use "in line with"), "underscore", "showcase"
- "serves as", "stands as" (just use "is")
- Excessive nominalization (prefer verbal constructions)
- "It should be noted that" (prefer "It is worth noting that")
- Starting sentences with "Importantly," or "Interestingly,"
- "and colleagues" in narrative citations (use "et al.")
- Synonym cycling: don't rotate synonyms for key terms to avoid repetition; repeating the same term is clearer
- Forcing ideas into groups of three for rhetorical effect

## Sentence Structure
- **Sentence length varies, and clarity governs.** Embedded clauses are welcome where they share a subject and the reader can hold the thread to the end; they stop working when the sentence stacks appositives, trails "which" clauses, or separates a modifier from what it modifies by a list. Short sentences carry emphasis and are used sparingly.
- A participial or gerund opener must take the sentence's subject as its agent.
- Semicolons connect closely related independent clauses. Colons introduce explanations or lists after a complete clause.
- Em dashes appear **rarely**. **Commas and parentheses share the work of asides**, and neither should carry all of them in a passage: where a sentence's commas are already marking its structure, the aside takes parentheses.

## Transitions
- **"However,"** (most frequent), **"Therefore,"**, **"Nevertheless,"**, **"In line with"** (bridge to prior work), **"Conversely,"**, **"Similarly,"**, **"Relatedly,"**
- Distinctive markers (don't overdo): **"In that,"** (meaning "regarding that"), **"It is worth noting that"**, **"In any case,"** (to acknowledge ambiguity while moving forward), **"To date,"**
- **Contrast connectives mark real turns.** "However", "Nevertheless" and "Conversely" appear only where the argument changes direction: a counter-finding, a limitation, an opposing account. Where the next sentence extends or specifies the last, use an additive link ("Relatedly,", "Similarly,", "Specifically,") or none.

## Paragraphs
- **A paragraph's first sentence names its move**: what the paragraph adds to the argument ("A further gap concerns the outcomes examined."; "The opposing account predicts that diversity lowers performance."). Avoid openers that only signal a turn without content ("This needs to be qualified, however.").

## Citations
- **High citation density**, integrated into the flow of the text.
- Provides **specific findings** from cited work: not "previous research found effects" but "a meta-analysis of 167 independent samples showed that..."
- Uses "et al." in narrative citations, not "and colleagues". Cites page numbers when quoting.
- When several studies support one point, the ones that carry the argument usually get their own sentence with their specific finding. Long semicolon chains of study summaries are hard to read; reserve them for brief, parallel lists.

## Prose and the numbers it describes
- **Every sentence summarising a table or figure is checked against it** before the draft is finished. Rhetorically parallel summaries ("X is more sensitive to A, Y is not more sensitive to B") are where a claim most often drifts from the data, because the parallelism is what makes it feel right.
- **Quantify in the body, not only in openings and abstracts.** "87% of the time", not "most of the time"; "about three times as often (49% against 15%)", not "several times more often". The same standard applied to cited work under Citations applies to our own results throughout.

## Footnotes
- Used actively for **nuanced asides, caveats, and technical details** that would disrupt the main text flow.
- Footnotes carry genuine content -- they are not perfunctory. Sometimes contain detailed methodological points or alternative interpretations.

## Quick Reference: Dos and Don'ts

### Do
- Use "we" (multi-author) or "I" (single-author) naturally
- Use British English by default
- Use commas and parentheses for asides (dashes only rarely)
- Provide specific quantitative details from cited studies
- Acknowledge counterarguments genuinely with "However," and "Nevertheless,"
- Use concrete examples to illustrate abstract points
- Use footnotes for substantive asides
- Report confidence intervals alongside point estimates
- Be honest about null, weak, or unexpected results
- Check every sentence that summarises a table or figure against it

### Don't
- Use "delve", "crucial", "novel", "robust" as generic praise
- Start sentences with "Importantly," or "Interestingly,"
- Over-hedge when evidence is clear
- Use passive voice where active reads naturally
- Use "It should be noted that" (prefer "It is worth noting that")
- Overclaim based on correlational evidence
- Use "and colleagues" in narrative citations

---

# Section-specific reference files

Consult these when drafting specific parts of a paper:

- `sections/introduction.md` -- introduction structure, theory-to-hypothesis transitions, argumentation, gap framing, contribution language
- `sections/methods.md` -- methods transparency, statistical reporting, open science conventions
- `sections/discussion.md` -- discussion opening/structure, limitations, practical implications, future directions, abstract style

  - **Confident:** "the evidence clearly favors", "it is clear that"
- Results that disconfirm expectations are reported openly: "Contrary to our expectation..."
- Uses concessive structures naturally: "While X is true, Y is also the case"
- Willing to state when evidence is inconclusive rather than forcing a narrative.
- When editing or rephrasing, the strength of a claim changes only by deliberate decision. Smoothing a sentence can quietly turn "shows" into "suggests" or "may" into "does".

## Vocabulary
- **Academic but accessible**: avoids unnecessarily complex vocabulary while maintaining precision.
- Slightly formal but not stiff; occasional colloquial touches in practitioner-oriented work ("window-dressing", "won't do").
- **Check that a category label covers all its members**: "two selection effects pull in opposite directions" where the second is not a selection effect; "the complementary quantity" followed two sentences later by "the two are not complements"; "bracket the range" for two values that both sit at its top.

### Words and constructions to avoid
- "delve", "crucial", "landscape" (as metaphor), "novel" (for own contribution), "robust" (as generic praise), "pivotal", "tapestry", "interplay", "intricacies"
- "align with" (use "in line with"), "underscore", "showcase"
- "serves as", "stands as" (just use "is")
- Excessive nominalization (prefer verbal constructions)
- "It should be noted that" (prefer "It is worth noting that")
- Starting sentences with "Importantly," or "Interestingly,"
- "and colleagues" in narrative citations (use "et al.")
- Synonym cycling: don't rotate synonyms for key terms to avoid repetition; repeating the same term is clearer
- Forcing ideas into groups of three for rhetorical effect

## Sentence Structure
- **Sentence length varies, and clarity governs.** Embedded clauses are welcome where they share a subject and the reader can hold the thread to the end; they stop working when the sentence stacks appositives, trails "which" clauses, or separates a modifier from what it modifies by a list. Short sentences carry emphasis and are used sparingly.
- A participial or gerund opener must take the sentence's subject as its agent.
- Semicolons connect closely related independent clauses. Colons introduce explanations or lists after a complete clause.
- Em dashes appear **rarely**. **Commas and parentheses share the work of asides**, and neither should carry all of them in a passage: where a sentence's commas are already marking its structure, the aside takes parentheses.

## Transitions
- **"However,"** (most frequent), **"Therefore,"**, **"Nevertheless,"**, **"In line with"** (bridge to prior work), **"Conversely,"**, **"Similarly,"**, **"Relatedly,"**
- Distinctive markers (don't overdo): **"In that,"** (meaning "regarding that"), **"It is worth noting that"**, **"In any case,"** (to acknowledge ambiguity while moving forward), **"To date,"**
- **Contrast connectives mark real turns.** "However", "Nevertheless" and "Conversely" appear only where the argument changes direction: a counter-finding, a limitation, an opposing account. Where the next sentence extends or specifies the last, use an additive link ("Relatedly,", "Similarly,", "Specifically,") or none.

## Paragraphs
- **A paragraph's first sentence names its move**: what the paragraph adds to the argument ("A further gap concerns the outcomes examined."; "The opposing account predicts that diversity lowers performance."). Avoid openers that only signal a turn without content ("This needs to be qualified, however.").

## Citations
- **High citation density**, integrated into the flow of the text.
- Provides **specific findings** from cited work: not "previous research found effects" but "a meta-analysis of 167 independent samples showed that..."
- Uses "et al." in narrative citations, not "and colleagues". Cites page numbers when quoting.
- When several studies support one point, the ones that carry the argument usually get their own sentence with their specific finding. Long semicolon chains of study summaries are hard to read; reserve them for brief, parallel lists.

## Prose and the numbers it describes
- **Every sentence summarising a table or figure is checked against it** before the draft is finished. Rhetorically parallel summaries ("X is more sensitive to A, Y is not more sensitive to B") are where a claim most often drifts from the data, because the parallelism is what makes it feel right.
- **Quantify in the body, not only in openings and abstracts.** "87% of the time", not "most of the time"; "about three times as often (49% against 15%)", not "several times more often". The same standard applied to cited work under Citations applies to our own results throughout.

## Footnotes
- Used actively for **nuanced asides, caveats, and technical details** that would disrupt the main text flow.
- Footnotes carry genuine content -- they are not perfunctory. Sometimes contain detailed methodological points or alternative interpretations.

## Quick Reference: Dos and Don'ts

### Do
- Use "we" (multi-author) or "I" (single-author) naturally
- Use British English by default
- Use commas and parentheses for asides (dashes only rarely)
- Provide specific quantitative details from cited studies
- Acknowledge counterarguments genuinely with "However," and "Nevertheless,"
- Use concrete examples to illustrate abstract points
- Use footnotes for substantive asides
- Report confidence intervals alongside point estimates
- Be honest about null, weak, or unexpected results
- Check every sentence that summarises a table or figure against it

### Don't
- Use "delve", "crucial", "novel", "robust" as generic praise
- Start sentences with "Importantly," or "Interestingly,"
- Over-hedge when evidence is clear
- Use passive voice where active reads naturally
- Use "It should be noted that" (prefer "It is worth noting that")
- Overclaim based on correlational evidence
- Use "and colleagues" in narrative citations

# Section-specific reference files

Consult these when drafting specific parts of a paper:

- `sections/introduction.md` -- introduction structure, theory-to-hypothesis transitions, argumentation, gap framing, contribution language
- `sections/methods.md` -- methods transparency, statistical reporting, open science conventions
- `sections/discussion.md` -- discussion opening/structure, limitations, practical implications, future directions, abstract style

manuscript/manuscript.template.md:94:The focal crossing environment used equal stratum shares, midpoint overlap, and advisor accuracy {{cross_a}} in both strata. The homogeneous control had advisor accuracies {{control_al}} and {{control_ah}}, retaining the same marginal accuracies but a positive advantage in both strata. These scenarios were selected in advance to contrast two mechanisms; they are not empirical prevalence estimates. manuscript/manuscript.template.md:102:Each learner selected the advisor for a positive score and the human for a negative score. Every rule was computed from the same paired records; the absolute rule uses only the advisor component. Calibration makes the strata psychologically interpretable but is not required for the weighting algebra.
manuscript/manuscript.template.md:114:All scenarios, budgets, and learners were retained. Grid comparisons used the prespecified regret tolerance {{grid_tolerance}} in proportion units ({{grid_tolerance_pp}} percentage points); they are descriptions of a chosen design, not statistical generalisations to a population of tasks.
manuscript/manuscript.template.md:128:In the crossing environment, uniform disagreement feedback gave the advisor a limiting selected accuracy of {{cross_d1_accuracy}}%, against the known marginal human benchmark of {{global_h_pct}}%. The paired contrast was positive at {{cross_d1_pair}}, correctly favouring the advisor. With high-confidence verification ratio {{h1_k}}, the selected advisor accuracy became {{cross_d4_accuracy}}% and the paired contrast became {{cross_d4_pair}}. Weighting restored the limiting contrast to {{cross_d4_ipw}}. The crossing environment has reversal threshold {{cross_threshold}}. At that ratio the limiting paired contrast is zero; at ratio {{h1_k}}, the registered cap also produces a zero limiting contrast. Capped adoption near chance in this scenario therefore reflects a deliberately reported neutral boundary, rather than evidence that this cap is generally a good compromise. Under random feedback, the absolute rule benefits from its supplied true human benchmark and avoids estimating human accuracy from the feedback sample.
manuscript/manuscript.template.md:150:{{extension_text}}
manuscript/manuscript.template.md:172:The accounts make distinct orderings on the raw-history crossing task. Absolute evaluation predicts adoption below chance after both uniform and confidence-selected disagreement feedback. Paired evaluation predicts adoption above chance under uniform selection and below chance under the crossing selective schedule. Selection-aware evaluation predicts above-chance adoption under both when histories are sufficiently informative. Display compliance predicts sensitivity to the supplied summary when it changes while the history is held fixed; it is not evidence that the corresponding statistic was computed without the display. An inferior-advisor control tests whether increased adoption reflects discrimination rather than general willingness to delegate.
manuscript/manuscript.template.md:178:The environments are stylised, not fitted to behavioural records or deployed systems. Discrete calibrated confidence strata omit noisy self-assessment and continuous difficulty. Correct feedback, stable source accuracies, known selection weights, and independent cases favour the statistical corrections. Estimated or misspecified sampling probabilities may substantially change their performance. Confidence-only weighting also requires selection to be independent of which source is right within a confidence stratum. If unmeasured difficulty or other within-stratum cues violate that condition, this correction generally fails. If a disagreement stratum is never verified, its contribution is not identified by these data; additional restrictions or positive random verification are required. The exploratory weight sensitivity preserves positive support and does not solve these missing-information cases. The fixed, exogenous feedback schedule also omits the feedback loops studied in adaptive sampling accounts [@denrell2001]. There is no evidence here about permanent abandonment, changes in trust over time, or why a person chooses to verify a case.

# PART A: Core Style Rules (always apply)

## Voice and Person
- **Default to "we" or "I"**, never use third person to refer to the researcher(s) or "we" in single-author papers (unless instructed otherwise for peer-review blinding).
- **Active voice** is strongly preferred but passive is acceptable in method sections where the agent is irrelevant.

## Spelling and Conventions
- **British English** by default (behaviour, organisation, standardised, practise, colour, analyse).
- APA formatting conventions followed for empirical papers.
- Oxford comma used consistently.
- Numbers: follows APA convention (words for numbers below 10 at the start of sentences, digits otherwise).

## Hedging and Epistemic Markers
- Claims are carefully **calibrated to match the strength of the evidence**:
  - **Tentative:** "it is possible that", "this suggests that", "might", "may", "appears to"
  - **Moderate:** "this is likely because", "evidently", "it appears clear that"
  - **Confident:** "the evidence clearly favors", "it is clear that"
- Results that disconfirm expectations are reported openly: "Contrary to our expectation..."
- Uses concessive structures naturally: "While X is true, Y is also the case"
- Willing to state when evidence is inconclusive rather than forcing a narrative.
- When editing or rephrasing, the strength of a claim changes only by deliberate decision. Smoothing a sentence can quietly turn "shows" into "suggests" or "may" into "does".

## Vocabulary
- **Academic but accessible**: avoids unnecessarily complex vocabulary while maintaining precision.
- Slightly formal but not stiff; occasional colloquial touches in practitioner-oriented work ("window-dressing", "won't do").
- **Check that a category label covers all its members**: "two selection effects pull in opposite directions" where the second is not a selection effect; "the complementary quantity" followed two sentences later by "the two are not complements"; "bracket the range" for two values that both sit at its top.

### Words and constructions to avoid
- "delve", "crucial", "landscape" (as metaphor), "novel" (for own contribution), "robust" (as generic praise), "pivotal", "tapestry", "interplay", "intricacies"
- "align with" (use "in line with"), "underscore", "showcase"
- "serves as", "stands as" (just use "is")
- Excessive nominalization (prefer verbal constructions)
- "It should be noted that" (prefer "It is worth noting that")
- Starting sentences with "Importantly," or "Interestingly,"
- "and colleagues" in narrative citations (use "et al.")
- Synonym cycling: don't rotate synonyms for key terms to avoid repetition; repeating the same term is clearer
- Forcing ideas into groups of three for rhetorical effect

## Sentence Structure
- **Sentence length varies, and clarity governs.** Embedded clauses are welcome where they share a subject and the reader can hold the thread to the end; they stop working when the sentence stacks appositives, trails "which" clauses, or separates a modifier from what it modifies by a list. Short sentences carry emphasis and are used sparingly.
- A participial or gerund opener must take the sentence's subject as its agent.
- Semicolons connect closely related independent clauses. Colons introduce explanations or lists after a complete clause.
- Em dashes appear **rarely**. **Commas and parentheses share the work of asides**, and neither should carry all of them in a passage: where a sentence's commas are already marking its structure, the aside takes parentheses.

## Transitions
- **"However,"** (most frequent), **"Therefore,"**, **"Nevertheless,"**, **"In line with"** (bridge to prior work), **"Conversely,"**, **"Similarly,"**, **"Relatedly,"**
- Distinctive markers (don't overdo): **"In that,"** (meaning "regarding that"), **"It is worth noting that"**, **"In any case,"** (to acknowledge ambiguity while moving forward), **"To date,"**
- **Contrast connectives mark real turns.** "However", "Nevertheless" and "Conversely" appear only where the argument changes direction: a counter-finding, a limitation, an opposing account. Where the next sentence extends or specifies the last, use an additive link ("Relatedly,", "Similarly,", "Specifically,") or none.

## Paragraphs
- **A paragraph's first sentence names its move**: what the paragraph adds to the argument ("A further gap concerns the outcomes examined."; "The opposing account predicts that diversity lowers performance."). Avoid openers that only signal a turn without content ("This needs to be qualified, however.").

## Citations
- **High citation density**, integrated into the flow of the text.
- Provides **specific findings** from cited work: not "previous research found effects" but "a meta-analysis of 167 independent samples showed that..."
- Uses "et al." in narrative citations, not "and colleagues". Cites page numbers when quoting.
- When several studies support one point, the ones that carry the argument usually get their own sentence with their specific finding. Long semicolon chains of study summaries are hard to read; reserve them for brief, parallel lists.

## Prose and the numbers it describes
- **Every sentence summarising a table or figure is checked against it** before the draft is finished. Rhetorically parallel summaries ("X is more sensitive to A, Y is not more sensitive to B") are where a claim most often drifts from the data, because the parallelism is what makes it feel right.
- **Quantify in the body, not only in openings and abstracts.** "87% of the time", not "most of the time"; "about three times as often (49% against 15%)", not "several times more often". The same standard applied to cited work under Citations applies to our own results throughout.

## Footnotes
- Used actively for **nuanced asides, caveats, and technical details** that would disrupt the main text flow.
- Footnotes carry genuine content -- they are not perfunctory. Sometimes contain detailed methodological points or alternative interpretations.

## Quick Reference: Dos and Don'ts

### Do
- Use "we" (multi-author) or "I" (single-author) naturally
- Use British English by default
- Use commas and parentheses for asides (dashes only rarely)
- Provide specific quantitative details from cited studies
- Acknowledge counterarguments genuinely with "However," and "Nevertheless,"
- Use concrete examples to illustrate abstract points
- Use footnotes for substantive asides
- Report confidence intervals alongside point estimates
- Be honest about null, weak, or unexpected results
- Check every sentence that summarises a table or figure against it

### Don't
- Use "delve", "crucial", "novel", "robust" as generic praise
- Start sentences with "Importantly," or "Interestingly,"
- Over-hedge when evidence is clear
- Use passive voice where active reads naturally
- Use "It should be noted that" (prefer "It is worth noting that")
- Overclaim based on correlational evidence
- Use "and colleagues" in narrative citations

- `sections/introduction.md` -- introduction structure, theory-to-hypothesis transitions, argumentation, gap framing, contribution language
- `sections/methods.md` -- methods transparency, statistical reporting, open science conventions
- `sections/discussion.md` -- discussion opening/structure, limitations, practical implications, future directions, abstract style

The protection depends on which disagreements are seen. Confidence-dependent selection changes the balance between contexts in which each source has an advantage. Pairing removes a mismatch between samples, but it does not remove a mismatch between the verified sample and the target population. This explains why adding the human's own hit rate to a feedback display may sometimes suffice and sometimes fail. The inference is conditional on the joint accuracy structure, not on an assumption that increased advisor acceptance is inherently desirable. Inferior advisors and exact ties were retained in the grid precisely because greater reliance is not itself an improvement.

Weighting adds a further distinction between estimation and action. Recovering the right limiting contrast does not guarantee a better finite-feedback adoption decision. An unweighted score may be distorted in magnitude yet preserve the appropriate sign, and selective verification can concentrate informative comparisons. Conversely, where selection reverses the sign, gathering more cases under the same uncorrected rule can increase confidence in the wrong source. Capped weights can reduce extreme contributions, but the focal neutral boundary and the full grid do not establish a general advantage for this cap. The cap was fixed prospectively and evaluated, not optimised to the observed results.

## A behavioural test that could reject the account

The immediate behavioural target is a decision-support intervention: whether displaying paired rather than absolute feedback changes global source adoption in the predicted way. A display experiment can test this claim but cannot by itself identify unaided cognitive updating. The proposed mapping is a substantive behavioural assumption, not a consequence of the accuracy tables.

A future test should separate raw-history and summary-display conditions. Generate histories under each assigned selection schedule and hold each history fixed across display conditions within that schedule. In raw-history conditions, show its ordered verified cases and their confidence strata without an aggregate score. Histories are not held identical across different selection schedules. Randomise whether the verification schedule is disclosed, and check understanding independently of the adoption outcome. In display conditions, retain the identical history while presenting advisor-only, paired, or adjusted summaries. These comparisons distinguish responses to supplied summaries from computation based on the history. They also reveal whether disclosing selection changes inference. The advisor-only and paired displays can imply opposite rankings for the same truthful history; the no-summary condition establishes which comparison people produce unaided.

A concrete prospective response family is $P(\mathrm{adopt}\mid S)=\lambda/2+(1-\lambda)\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\beta S)$, with $\beta>0$ and $0\leq\lambda<1$. The candidate scores $S$ are the absolute, paired, and selection-adjusted summaries defined above. This response family is an exploratory specification for future model comparison, not a fitted model or an additional simulated result. Within a preregistered task, sensitivity and lapse parameters must be shared across sampling schedules; otherwise arbitrary condition-specific parameters could absorb the predicted differences.

The accounts make distinct orderings on the raw-history crossing task. Absolute evaluation predicts adoption below chance after both uniform and confidence-selected disagreement feedback. Paired evaluation predicts adoption above chance under uniform selection and below chance under the crossing selective schedule. Selection-aware evaluation predicts above-chance adoption under both when histories are sufficiently informative. Display compliance predicts sensitivity to the supplied summary when it changes while the history is held fixed; it is not evidence that the corresponding statistic was computed without the display. An inferior-advisor control tests whether increased adoption reflects discrimination rather than general willingness to delegate.

Future inference should use the likelihood of held-out choices to compare the prespecified response models, alongside directional intervals for the display-by-selection interaction. A precise reversed ordering rejects the corresponding directional account; an interval concentrated near no interaction rejects a prespecified practically relevant display effect. This paper does not invent a human effect-size threshold from simulated decision makers: a future empirical protocol must fix that threshold, power, comprehension criteria, and model-comparison rule before collecting outcomes. Asymmetric treatment of self and advisor errors, numeracy, trust in adjusted statistics, and experimental demand remain candidate explanations. The raw-history and disclosure conditions are needed because a successful display intervention alone cannot adjudicate among them.

## Scope of the inference

The environments are stylised, not fitted to behavioural records or deployed systems. Discrete calibrated confidence strata omit noisy self-assessment and continuous difficulty. Correct feedback, stable source accuracies, known selection weights, and independent cases favour the statistical corrections. Estimated or misspecified sampling probabilities may substantially change their performance. Confidence-only weighting also requires selection to be independent of which source is right within a confidence stratum. If unmeasured difficulty or other within-stratum cues violate that condition, this correction generally fails. If a disagreement stratum is never verified, its contribution is not identified by these data; additional restrictions or positive random verification are required. The exploratory weight sensitivity preserves positive support and does not solve these missing-information cases. The fixed, exogenous feedback schedule also omits the feedback loops studied in adaptive sampling accounts [@denrell2001]. There is no evidence here about permanent abandonment, changes in trust over time, or why a person chooses to verify a case.

Global adoption is appropriate for a constrained handoff, such as selecting one source for a batch when casewise routing is unavailable. If routing by confidence is possible, the action space changes. The confidence-contingent oracle achieves {{routing_cross_pct}}% in the crossing environment compared with {{global_a_pct}}% for the best fixed source, and {{routing_control_pct}}% in the homogeneous control. Within-stratum paired estimates preserve each stratum’s sign without between-stratum weighting, although sparse strata still create finite-sample uncertainty. The present results do not show that global weighting is preferable to learning such a routing policy.

The resource comparison is equally specific. Equal label counts make sense when obtaining truth is the expensive step, but selective verification can require substantially more opportunities. Where time, delay, or opportunity costs dominate, equal-label comparisons alone do not establish the preferable policy. The model reports this cost rather than attaching an arbitrary exchange rate to labels and opportunities.

Finally, selection adjustment here is a benchmark available to a software display, not necessarily a plausible mental calculation. Its relation to human choice remains open, and the theoretical distinction may prove more useful for feedback design than for explaining existing behaviour. The resulting recommendation is correspondingly limited: evaluate advisor and self on matched cases, then establish whether those matched cases preserve the comparative ordering relevant to the next decision. Statistical correction is one possible response when they do not; its finite-feedback cost must also be assessed.

# Transparency and declarations

Review this revised computational Theory Article as round 2 (maximum3 rounds). Evaluate the current manuscript and the accompanying response log critically. Identify only issues that remain, distinguish major from minor, and number every actionable comment. Do not invent reference metadata. Full citeproc-rendered bibliography is included. Code and results were independently checked by exact convolution; all registered contrasts remain, with numerical—not human empirical—interpretation. Reviewer-requested exact opportunity-budget and weight-misspecification analyses are explicitly exploratory. Distinguish objections to the chosen bounded global-adoption task from errors within that task, and assess whether scope is sufficiently justified. Evaluate the future behavioural extension for honest refutability, without treating it as an executed experiment.
This is an autonomous local research draft; no submission is authorised, and the intended human author has not yet endorsed it. Record human accountability/public archiving as future submission requirements, but do not ask the automated author to falsely certify human oversight or upload material. Initial preregistration was a prospective git commitment as explicitly requested, not a public registry. Its limitation must remain explicit.
Do not edit files or use external tools. Give a verdict and state whether any substantive major issue remains after the revisions. Do not suppress concerns to meet the review limit. End with the answer under ## Answer.

## Exploratory checks requested in review

{{exploratory_text}}

{{matched_table}}

{{extension_text}}

*Table 3. Matched focal comparisons, exact regret in percentage points. These descriptive exact checks use the same budgets and ratios in both environments; they do not change the registered contrasts.*

# Discussion

{{discussion_opening}}

The first implication concerns the target of feedback. When advice and an initial judgement agree, the verified truth cannot favour one response over the other. Under uniform disagreement sampling, comparing the two sources on the same cases therefore retains the information required for global ranking. A low selected advisor hit rate can coexist with a useful advisor because the decision maker's own accuracy on those cases is lower still. This qualification complements sampling accounts of mistrust [@denrell2005; @fetchenhauer2010]: representativeness of observed outcomes is not equally necessary for every judgement.

The protection depends on which disagreements are seen. Confidence-dependent selection changes the balance between contexts in which each source has an advantage. Pairing removes a mismatch between samples, but it does not remove a mismatch between the verified sample and the target population. This explains why adding the human's own hit rate to a feedback display may sometimes suffice and sometimes fail. The inference is conditional on the joint accuracy structure, not on an assumption that increased advisor acceptance is inherently desirable. Inferior advisors and exact ties were retained in the grid precisely because greater reliance is not itself an improvement.

Weighting adds a further distinction between estimation and action. Recovering the right limiting contrast does not guarantee a better finite-feedback adoption decision. An unweighted score may be distorted in magnitude yet preserve the appropriate sign, and selective verification can concentrate informative comparisons. Conversely, where selection reverses the sign, gathering more cases under the same uncorrected rule can increase confidence in the wrong source. Capped weights can reduce extreme contributions, but the focal neutral boundary and the full grid do not establish a general advantage for this cap. The cap was fixed prospectively and evaluated, not optimised to the observed results.

## A behavioural test that could reject the account

The immediate behavioural target is a decision-support intervention: whether displaying paired rather than absolute feedback changes global source adoption in the predicted way. A display experiment can test this claim but cannot by itself identify unaided cognitive updating. The proposed mapping is a substantive behavioural assumption, not a consequence of the accuracy tables.

A future test should separate raw-history and summary-display conditions. Generate histories under each assigned selection schedule and hold each history fixed across display conditions within that schedule. In raw-history conditions, show its ordered verified cases and their confidence strata without an aggregate score. Histories are not held identical across different selection schedules. Randomise whether the verification schedule is disclosed, and check understanding independently of the adoption outcome. In display conditions, retain the identical history while presenting advisor-only, paired, or adjusted summaries. These comparisons distinguish responses to supplied summaries from computation based on the history. They also reveal whether disclosing selection changes inference. The advisor-only and paired displays can imply opposite rankings for the same truthful history; the no-summary condition establishes which comparison people produce unaided.

A concrete prospective response family is $P(\mathrm{adopt}\mid S)=\lambda/2+(1-\lambda)\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\beta S)$, with $\beta>0$ and $0\leq\lambda<1$. The candidate scores $S$ are the absolute, paired, and selection-adjusted summaries defined above. This response family is an exploratory specification for future model comparison, not a fitted model or an additional simulated result. Within a preregistered task, sensitivity and lapse parameters must be shared across sampling schedules; otherwise arbitrary condition-specific parameters could absorb the predicted differences.

The accounts make distinct orderings on the raw-history crossing task. Absolute evaluation predicts adoption below chance after both uniform and confidence-selected disagreement feedback. Paired evaluation predicts adoption above chance under uniform selection and below chance under the crossing selective schedule. Selection-aware evaluation predicts above-chance adoption under both when histories are sufficiently informative. Display compliance predicts sensitivity to the supplied summary when it changes while the history is held fixed; it is not evidence that the corresponding statistic was computed without the display. An inferior-advisor control tests whether increased adoption reflects discrimination rather than general willingness to delegate.

The protection depends on which disagreements are seen. Confidence-dependent selection changes the balance between contexts in which each source has an advantage. Pairing removes a mismatch between samples, but it does not remove a mismatch between the verified sample and the target population. This explains why adding the human's own hit rate to a feedback display may sometimes suffice and sometimes fail. The inference is conditional on the joint accuracy structure, not on an assumption that increased advisor acceptance is inherently desirable.
